creator: Yuzhen Huang, Yuzhuo Bai, Zhihao Zhu, Junlei Zhang, Jinghan Zhang, Tangjun Su, Junteng Liu, Chuancheng Lv, Yikai Zhang, Jiayi Lei, Yao Fu, Maosong Sun, Junxian He (Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Tsinghua University, University of Edinburgh, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology)
description: C-Eval is the first comprehensive Chinese evaluation suite designed to assess advanced knowledge and reasoning abilities of foundation models in a Chinese context. It consists of 13,948 multiple-choice exam questions spanning 52 diverse disciplines across four difficulty levels: middle school, high school, college, and professional. The questions range from humanities to science and engineering, and are accompanied by C-Eval HARD, a subset of particularly challenging subjects requiring advanced reasoning abilities.
name: C-Eval
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotators are the paper authors, affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Tsinghua University, University of Edinburgh, and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Questions underwent several rounds of human validation by the authors, with cross-validation of collected data. Option bias was analyzed by examining the distribution of correct answers across choices (A: 22.9%, B: 26.0%, C: 26.4%, D: 24.7%), which showed relatively small fluctuations similar to MMLU. To verify option bias in model responses, choices were permuted in 5 distinct permutations per question and evaluated on ChatGPT, ChatGLM-6B, and ChatGLM2-6B, showing low variance.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Manual annotation by the paper authors (no external crowdsourcing platform used)
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Questions were parsed and annotated by the authors into a structured format. For subjects with complex mathematical notations, LaTeX formats were manually converted. The questions underwent several rounds of human validation by the authors. Development set exemplars (5 per subject) were annotated with explanations to enable few-shot chain-of-thought settings: GPT-4 was first prompted to generate step-by-step explanations, then the generated explanations were manually revised by the authors.
rai:dataBiases: The paper acknowledges that English benchmarks tend to exhibit geographical biases towards the domestic knowledge of the regions that produce them. C-Eval was designed to address this by focusing on Chinese-specific knowledge. To mitigate data contamination bias, questions were collected from mock exams or small-scale local exams rather than official national exams, and mostly sourced from PDF/Word documents rather than plain text, to reduce the risk of LLM pretraining data leakage. The paper also notes that there are fluctuations in the distribution of correct answer options (A: 22.9%, B: 26.0%, C: 26.4%, D: 24.7%), similar to MMLU.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected from mock exams and small-scale local exams freely available on the internet, as well as past exam questions from top universities in China shared by students. A minor fraction of college questions are mock questions for the national graduate entrance exam sourced from the Weipu website. The primary format was PDF or Microsoft Word documents, with a minor fraction as web pages.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists primarily of PDF and Microsoft Word documents containing mock exam questions and past exam questions, sourced from the internet and the Weipu website. A minor fraction came as web pages.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: C-Eval, along with all English-language benchmarks, is far from perfect for LLM evaluation. There are many other abilities such as reasoning over and calling APIs, as well as multiple aspects that extend beyond accuracy, including safety, bias, and robustness. The benchmark only uses multiple-choice format, which may not capture all aspects of LLM capabilities.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: PDF documents were initially processed into text. All questions were parsed — automatically when possible, and otherwise manually by the authors — into a structured format. For subjects with complex mathematical notations, LaTeX formats were manually applied. Questions were standardized to include exactly four choices (questions with fewer than four options were eliminated; incorrect choices were randomly dropped for questions with more than four options). All questions went through deduplication and cleaning. LaTeX notations were ensured to compile without syntax errors. Questions were randomly split into development, validation, and test sets within each subject at a 1:9 ratio for validation and test.
rai:dataSocialImpact: C-Eval aims to narrow the gap between Chinese LLM development and evaluation, fostering the development and growth of foundation models for Chinese users. It provides a benchmark that reflects Chinese cultural, historical, and legal knowledge, addressing the underrepresentation of Chinese language in existing LLM evaluation.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating advanced knowledge and reasoning abilities of foundation models in a Chinese context; assessing LLMs across multiple dimensions (STEM, humanities, social science, and other areas); benchmarking Chinese and English-oriented LLMs; hyperparameter tuning using the validation split; few-shot and chain-of-thought evaluation settings.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: GPT-4 was used to automatically generate step-by-step explanations for the development split exemplars, which were then manually revised by the authors.

evidence.isLiveDataset: While ground-truth labels of the development and validation splits are released, we keep the labels of the test split private. This is to ensure the fair use of the C-E VAL, as the C-E VAL data may unconsciously be included in pretraining data due to web crawling.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: The primary source of our data is mock exams freely available on the internet. In addition, a portion of the college-level questions are past exam questions from top universities in China, publicly shared by the students. A minor fraction of college questions are mock questions for the national graduate entrance exam, sourced from the Weipu website – these questions are not freely available to the public, and we have obtained their authorization to include around 2000 such questions into C-E VAL.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: The collected data come in various formats, primarily as PDF or Microsoft Word documents and a minor fraction as web pages. PDF documents are initially processed into text. All questions are subsequently parsed – automatically when possible, and otherwise manually by the authors – into a structured format.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The collected data come in various formats, primarily as PDF or Microsoft Word documents and a minor fraction as web pages. PDF documents are initially processed into text.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: All questions are subsequently parsed – automatically when possible, and otherwise manually by the authors – into a structured format. All the questions in C-E VAL are processed to include exactly four choices. Most of the original questions were accompanied by four choices already, and we eliminate questions with fewer than four options and randomly drop incorrect choices for questions with more than four options. All questions also go through the standard data preprocessing pipeline, such as deduplication and cleaning.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Following this, the questions undergo several rounds of human validation by the authors, and all the L ATEX notations are ensured to be complied without syntax errors. We process at least around 200 questions for each subject, and randomly split the questions into a development set, a validation set, and a test set within each subject.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: All questions are subsequently parsed – automatically when possible, and otherwise manually by the authors – into a structured format, as exemplified in Figure 2. For subjects with complex mathematical notations such as many subjects in the STEM category, we manually convert them into standard L ATEX formats.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Specifically, we first prompt GPT-4 to generate step-by-step explanation to explain the ground-truth answer, then we manually revise the generated explanations to obtain the final explanations.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: English benchmarks tend to exhibit geographical biases towards the domestic knowledge of the regions that produce them. To mitigate this risk, we collect our data either from mock exams or from small-scale local exams, such as those available online from specific high schools. This deviates from previous work that built benchmarks using the exact questions from official national exams.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: We also note that, C-E VAL, along with all the English-language benchmarks, is far from perfect for LLM evaluation. There are many other abilities such as reasoning over and calling APIs, as well as multiple aspects that extend beyond accuracy, including safety, bias, and robustness. We leave further exploration on their evaluation for future work.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: We anticipate C-E VAL will help analyze important strengths and shortcomings of foundation models, and foster their development and growth for Chinese users. In addition to its use as a whole, we envision C-E VAL as a suite of benchmarks, subsets of which could be separately utilized to assess certain model abilities of interest and analyze important strengths and limitations of foundation models.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: To narrow the gap between Chinese LLM development and evaluation, we present C-E VAL, the first comprehensive Chinese evaluation suite to thoroughly assess LLMs' advanced knowledge and reasoning abilities in a Chinese context. We anticipate C-E VAL will help analyze important strengths and shortcomings of foundation models, and foster their development and growth for Chinese users.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: Data collection, annotation, and initial validation: Yuzhen Huang, Yuzhuo Bai, Zhihao Zhu, Junlei Zhang, Jinghan Zhang, Tangjun Su, Junteng Liu, Yikai Zhang, and Jiayi Lei collected the first version of the data, including some necessary manual annotation from PDF or Word documents. They then cross-validated the collected data.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Following this, the questions undergo several rounds of human validation by the authors, and all the L ATEX notations are ensured to be complied without syntax errors. We admit that there are fluctuations in the proportion of different options. However, these fluctuations are relatively small around a random 25% level and similar to MMLU.
